analysis.one_liner: Offers House candidates full public campaign financing in exchange for refusing all private campaign money.
analysis.headline: Referred to three House committees in July 1997, the bill never got a markup or a floor vote and died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have created a voluntary 'clean money' system for House races. A candidate who collected a set number of small $5 qualifying contributions from voters could agree to take no private money and no personal wealth in the campaign, and instead receive a public grant sized to typical winning House campaigns, plus free TV and radio time and discounted ad rates. The bill also would have banned national parties from raising unlimited 'soft money,' required faster disclosure of big independent and 'issue' ads, and strengthened the Federal Election Commission with random audits and faster enforcement.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters, candidates without personal fortunes or access to wealthy donor networks, and taxpayers in their role as citizens. Candidates who qualified would receive public grants instead of having to raise money from monied interests; the bill's own findings state the goal of removing wealth as a determinant of political influence and making House elections more competitive for challengers [S3]. It also would have cut off the 'soft money' channel that let national parties raise unlimited contributions outside the normal limits [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters and candidates without wealthy donor networks

how_it_helps.text: Creates a full public financing option: a candidate who collects 1,500 five-dollar qualifying contributions (or 150 percent of that for minor-party candidates) can certify as a clean money candidate and receive a grant based on the national average spent by recent winning House candidates — 60 percent of that base for a general election, more if opposed by heavy outside spending [S3].
Clean money candidates must reject all other contributions and cannot use personal or family wealth, and face civil penalties of up to 10 times the amount for spending outside the system [S3].
Provides clean candidates with free broadcast time (30 minutes for primaries, 75 minutes for general elections in prime-time windows) and television rates capped at half the lowest unit rate [S3].

Bans national party committees from soliciting or spending unregulated 'soft money,' bars party donations to tax-exempt groups, and requires State parties to fund federal-election activity with federally limited money [S2].

Expands disclosure: large independent expenditures and 'issue advertisements' naming a candidate must be reported within 48 hours, and campaign ads must carry clear on-screen and spoken 'who paid for this' statements [S3].
Restructures the FEC with commissioners limited to a single six-year term, random post-election audits, authority to seek injunctions, and expedited handling of late-election complaints [S2].
Bars incumbent members from using taxpayer-funded mass mailings (the franking privilege) in their election year, a perk that can double as free campaign advertising [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers fund the public grants, through appropriations of 'such sums as are necessary' to a new House of Representatives Election Fund [S3]. Broadcasters bear the cost of mandated free airtime and discounted ad rates. National and state party committees lose the unlimited soft-money channel, and large individual and corporate donors lose the private financing route for any race with a clean-money candidate.

drawbacks.text: The public financing is funded by open-ended taxpayer appropriations, so the direct cost of House campaigns shifts onto the federal budget [S3].

A candidate who opts in must take no private contributions and cannot spend personal wealth, so self-funded or heavily funded opponents are constrained only by matching grants that cap at 200 percent of the clean money amount — critics could argue this trades one fairness problem for another and invites First Amendment challenges [S3].

Matching funds that automatically rise when outside groups spend against a clean candidate can push total spending upward rather than down, and mandatory free airtime and half-price rates impose a real cost on stations that would likely face legal challenge [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential upside is large: public financing of House campaigns, party soft money shut down, faster disclosure of shadow ads, and a stronger election regulator, all aimed at loosening the link between money and legislative access. The costs are a new federal outlay and burdens on broadcasters and parties, and the design has genuine weak points — the opt-in structure leaves a two-track system where unlimited private spending against a clean candidate only triggers capped matching grants. On balance the benefits for voters outweigh the costs, but the bill never got far enough for any of this to be tested or amended.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in July 1997 and split among three House committees, each of which referred it to a subcommittee; no committee ever reported it and no vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Rep. John Tierney introduced the Clean Money, Clean Elections Act on July 17, 1997, with 34 cosponsors (33 Democrats and 1 Independent) [S4] [S5].
That same day the Speaker referred it to three committees — House Oversight, Commerce, and Government Reform and Oversight — 'for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker' [S5].

Five days later, the Government Reform and Commerce committees each sent it to a subcommittee, the Subcommittee on Government Management, Information and Technology and the Subcommittee on Telecommunications, Trade, and Consumer Protection [S5].
The only other recorded activity was the sponsor's introductory remarks in September 1997 [S5].
No committee reported the bill, no floor vote was ever held, and the bill died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent members and their large campaign donors are better off, since the private fundraising system and unlimited party soft money stayed in place; national party committees also kept the soft-money channel, and broadcasters avoided the free-airtime and discounted-rate mandates.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Incumbents, large donors, party committees, broadcasters

for.name: John Tierney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it in September 1997.

for.name: 33 House Democrats and 1 Independent
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, including members from across the liberal-to-moderate range of the House Democratic caucus and Independent Bernie Sanders.

against.name: Newt Gingrich
against.what_they_did: Held the referral authority under which the bill went to three committees 'for a period to be subsequently determined'; the bill was never scheduled for House floor action during the Congress.

against.name: Thomas J. Bliley Jr.
against.what_they_did: Received the referral covering the bill's broadcast provisions, sent it to the Telecommunications subcommittee, and never brought it to a markup or vote.

against.name: Dan Burton
against.role: Chair, House Government Reform and Oversight Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral covering the bill's FEC restructuring provisions, sent it to the Government Management subcommittee, and never brought it to a markup or vote.

against.name: Bill Thomas
against.what_they_did: Received the primary referral of the campaign-finance bill and never scheduled a markup or vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 34 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or the lone Independent, and every committee chairman holding the bill was a Republican; no Republican cosponsor is listed, and no roll-call vote was ever taken to break down support further.

industries.note: The bill would have required stations to give clean-money candidates substantial free airtime in prime windows and sell them TV ads at half the lowest rate, with limits on preemption [S3]. Broadcasters' interest in this bill ran against the public benefit of a campaign-finance system that did not depend on paid advertising.

industries.industry: Political parties (national and state party committees)
industries.note: The bill would have banned national parties from raising or spending unlimited soft money, barred donations to tax-exempt groups, and capped party coordinated spending in races with a clean candidate [S2] [S3]. Parties' interest was in preserving the unregulated funding channel the bill targeted.

industries.industry: Large campaign donors and monied interests
industries.note: Clean-money candidates would take no private contributions, so wealthy donors and interest groups would lose their funding lever in any race with a participating candidate; expanded 48-hour disclosure of big independent and issue advertisements would also expose their spending [S3]. The bill's own findings describe the current system as giving monied interests disproportionate influence [S3].

industries.industry: Political advertising and direct mail industries
industries.note: Clean candidates could not buy broadcast ads with private funds and seed money could not fund TV or radio spots, reducing the paid-ad market in races with clean candidates, though private-money candidates and outside groups could still buy ads under new disclosure rules [S3].
